text: ← Advanced contents AVAILABLE CHAPTERS WHAT YOU WILL LEARNDerive scale height from vertical balance, define the ν = αcsH convention, and connect steady mass, angular-momentum, and energy budgets. Connect to foundations: Stellar structure and the mass–luminosity relation ↗ Compare solution assumptions and boundary data in the solution library ↗ 01Specify transport strength without choosing its cause The transport chapter related inward accretion to outward angular-momentum flux. A viscous-type disk prescribes an effective kinematic viscosity ν instead of deriving its stresses microscopically; ν need not represent molecular collisions. ν ≡ αcsH, [ν] = m² s−1 This equation defines our alpha convention. It is a dimensional closure using a velocity cs and length H, not a derivation of alpha’s value. MRI, self-gravity, winds, or other mechanisms must be assessed separately. 02Derive thickness from vertical balance For a thin disk dominated by a central mass M, vertical gravity is −ΩK²z at |z| ≪ r, with ΩK² = GM/r³. A vertically isothermal closure P = ρcs² gives a Gaussian density profile. cs²d lnρdz = −ΩK²z ρ(z) = ρ(0)exp(−z²2H²), H = csΩK H is a Gaussian scale height, not a sharp edge. Substitution gives ν = αH²ΩK. A small aspect ratio H/r makes radial viscous evolution slow compared with orbital motion. tν ∼ r²ν = 1α(rH)²ΩK−1 03Keep the stress sign and alpha convention explicit Define W as vertically integrated stress transporting angular momentum outward, with positive sign for outward transport. Keplerian shear has dΩ/dr < 0, so W = −νΣr dΩ/dr is positive for positive ν. Surface density Σ has different units from volume density ρ. W = −νΣrdΩdr = 32νΣΩ, 𝒢 = 2πr²W = 3πνΣj Our viscosity convention gives W = (3/2)αΣcs². A convention defining stress directly as αΣcs² has a different alpha by a factor of 3/2. The same symbol does not guarantee the same numerical normalization. 04Connect the torque to a steady accretion rate Assume steady flow with no wind or mass sources and zero torque at an inner radius rin. Combine 𝒢 = Ṁ(j−jin) with j = √(GMr) to obtain the relation between viscosity, surface density, and accretion. νΣ = Ṁ3π[1−√(rinr)] r ≫ rin : Ṁ ≈ 3πνΣ, vr ≈ −3ν2r The panel assumes a one-solar-mass central object and Σ = 100 g cm−2, with aspect ratio, alpha, and radius as inputs. It does not solve a radiative equilibrium for temperature or surface density. Changing alpha alone is different from recomputing an entire disk structure. 05Where is the released energy radiated? Dissipation combines stress with shear. If a thin disk radiates the dissipated energy locally from its two faces, the flux from one face is given below. Advected heat and energy carried off by a wind are neglected. 2F = νΣ(rdΩdr)² = 94νΣΩ² F(r) = 3GMṀ8πr³[1−√(rinr)] L = ∫rin∞4πrF(r)dr = GMṀ2rin The area 4πr dr includes both faces. The effective temperature defined by F = σSBTeff⁴ need not equal the internal temperature setting H. Additional emission from a stellar surface or boundary layer is not included in this disk luminosity. 06What alpha does not determine Alpha provides a useful closure, but does not replace a theory of the transport mechanism. Ideal-MHD MRI cannot simply be imposed when gas is poorly coupled to fields; a disk dominated by vertical wind torques is not fully described by radial viscosity alone. MRI examines linear extraction of differential-rotation energy; Toomre Q examines linear gravitational instability. Neither by itself uniquely specifies a saturated alpha. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. At fixed radius, central mass, H/r, and surface density, triple alpha. Far from the inner edge of a steady disk, what happens to viscosity, accretion rate, and viscous time? Show the answer and reasoning Viscosity and Ṁ ≈ 3πνΣ triple; tν ∼ r²/ν falls to one-third. Temperature and surface density have not been allowed to change simultaneously. The comparison requires an explicit convention and fixed inputs.
